improvement_notes: State explicitly that the shortest-path guarantee depends not only on an admissible heuristic but also on the search implementation and termination rule; the provided implementation is appropriate because it permits improved costs to be reconsidered.

Add the expected numerical output or at least the expected optimal path cost for the supplied grid. This would make the Python lab easier to verify and would expose accidental map or coordinate edits.
Clarify that the code's `expanded` count measures popped-and-accepted nodes, not necessarily every unique node discovered, and that comparisons between algorithms depend on the tie-breaking policy.

The weighted-A* experiment would benefit from a warning that increasing the heuristic weight changes search behavior but does not guarantee a particular degree of speedup or path degradation on this specific map.

In the terrain-cost challenge, define whether the cost of a cell is charged on entry, and provide a small terrain-cost data structure or pseudocode so beginners can implement the modification without guessing.
Name the standard diagonal heuristic, octile distance, in the optional extension. This would turn a good conceptual prompt into a more complete technical bridge.
Reduce minor repetition among the heuristic, admissibility, common-mistake, and quiz explanations. The lesson is strong but could be shortened slightly without losing foundational coverage.
Add one explicit question connecting the worked example to the code: ask students to identify which dictionary value corresponds to g(n) and which priority expression computes f(n).

The generated `diagram.png` section gives general instructions for reading a visual but does not identify the specific blocks or relationships shown. Add two or three visual callouts tied directly to A*, the controller, and replanning.

Consider explaining that Manhattan distance remains admissible with nonuniform terrain costs only when scaled by a valid lower bound on per-step cost; otherwise the challenge wording may encourage an oversimplified implementation.
